A new guide from The Ambrose Group explains the 2027 Harris County property tax protest process, from the notice and filing deadline through HCAD’s online tools, the ARB hearing and the appeal options that follow, with added detail for commercial owners. 
 Jersey Village, United States, October 22, 2026 -- The Ambrose Group, a Texas property tax consulting and appraisal firm, has released a guide to the 2027 property tax protest season in Harris County. The guide was written by Daniel Ambrose, MAI, Executive Vice President of Tax Services. It covers the steps from the appraisal notice to a final appeal and is available on the company website at https://theambrosegroup.com/harris-county-property-tax-protest-2027/ .
 The filing date comes from Section 41.44 of the Texas Tax Code. Owners get until May 15, or until the 30th day after HCAD mails the notice if that comes later. Next year May 15 lands on a Saturday, and a separate rule pushes weekend deadlines to the following Monday, May 17. Ambrose does not recommend waiting that long. His advice is to file the same week the notice arrives and to treat Friday, May 14, as the real cutoff, since a paper protest is judged by its postmark.
 The Harris Central Appraisal District, or HCAD, offers two online paths. Owners can file through iFile using the number printed on the notice. Owners of single-family homes can also opt into iSettle, which lets them upload evidence within five calendar days and receive a settlement offer by email. According to the guide, iSettle is not available for commercial, industrial or multifamily property. Those owners file, request an informal meeting with an HCAD appraiser and prepare for the Appraisal Review Board.
 The guide explains who has to prove what. At the ARB, the appraisal district must establish the property’s value by a preponderance of the evidence, and that standard can rise in certain cases when owners file specific evidence at least 14 days before the hearing. For commercial owners, the guide lists the documents that tend to move a value: income and expense statements, a current rent roll, adjusted sale and lease comparables, and records of condition as of January 1. “Texas is a non-disclosure state, so the district is guessing at commercial sale prices,” Ambrose writes.
 Some owners bring an outside appraisal to the hearing. Ambrose explains why that can help. “An independent appraisal reports what the evidence supports,” he writes. “It isn’t written to hit a target, which is why it carries weight.” He also pushes back on a common belief that a value cannot drop below the previous year’s number. “Last year’s value is not the floor either,” he writes.
 Commercial owners also face a possible shift in 2027. Texas currently caps yearly appraisal increases at 20% for non-homestead real property worth about $5.3 million or less. The Texas Comptroller says that cap, found in Tax Code Section 23.231, ends on December 31, 2026. Unless the Legislature renews it, next year’s notices on those properties can show their full market value, and some owners may see bigger jumps than they are used to.
 Once the ARB rules, owners usually get 60 days from receiving its order to choose binding arbitration or a lawsuit in district court, and owners of non-industrial property valued above $1 million can appeal to the State Office of Administrative Hearings. The guide notes that undisputed taxes must still be paid on time, regardless of the route. A broader overview of the statewide process is available at https://theambrosegroup.com/texas-property-tax-protest-guide/ and the firm’s hearing representation is described at https://theambrosegroup.com/appraisal-review-board/ on the same site.
 About The Ambrose Group:
 The Ambrose Group is a Texas real estate consulting firm based in Jersey Village that has provided property tax consulting, appraisal, cost segregation and brokerage services since 1994. The company profile at https://theambrosegroup.com/about-real-estate-company/ covers its history and team.
